question: Why did corner wind strain Citicorp's braces more than head-on wind?
answer: When wind hits the corner, it splits into two pushes of F/√2, one on each face. In half the diagonal braces these pushes cancel, and in the other half they add to 2 × F/√2 ≈ 1.41 F. That is 40% above the head-on load LeMessurier had calculated.
move: Wind on the corner, not on a face, loaded Citicorp's braces hardest: 40% more.

web.label: A tower with diagonal braces and a wind arrow you drag around it. Question: why does wind hitting the corner strain the braces more than wind head-on? The force splits into two pushes that add to about 1.41 times the head-on load.

source: Veritasium, “This Skyscraper Was Days From Collapsing And No One Knew” (YouTube, 2025)
